title: Looking for resources
author: Aggressive-Fan-4230
selftext:
I’m not now to development but am new to game dev. I want to try my hand and making my own personal (not for steam) game to learn the concepts as I go. 

I was hoping I could have AI vibe code it most of the way while I learn what it’s doing and understand the workflows. 

I can’t seem to find a resource here that points you at what tools to use and what’s best atm.

I’m used to the ai chatbot in the right panel as I code a react app. Was hoping I might find something similar that can get you equally the way through without diving deep into something specific if I don’t want to.

comments.author: Fuzzzy420
comments.body:
Humblebundle.com -> Software -> find Tutorials and assets, changing weekly (more or less)

There are no big resources yet because it's new. Most people offer the knowledge for money, ai goldrush.

replies.author: Aggressive-Fan-4230
replies.body: Yeah I just dislike the “heres this very specific tutorial” type things because as a new person you don’t know what you will actually need and what’s too in depth for you. The idea with AI is that it would put you in the drivers seat and you can actually do something

replies.author: Brettinabox
replies.body: I feel that, you get locked in to however the teacher is doing it, then you have to watch more and more teachers to really get a good understanding. It is self-learning, but ai chat has come far enough that it is a tutor.

replies.author: Fuzzzy420
replies.body:
Just start somewhere and learn along the way. Don't expect your first titles to go anywhere. People learn game Devs for a long time. Don't expect to get it perfect the first time. 
Believe me I did like many others, it's so easy to lose the scope of things, be aware of affirmation and let ai roast your decisions. 

Start with small ideas, build them and publish them no matter how shitty they are. You want to learn publishing as well and you get good feedback. 
Just don't post it on Reddit, like: look what I did, but rather ask how to improve specific things or you get roasted.

replies.author: Aggressive-Fan-4230
replies.body: I mean yeah but also I’m mainly asking how to do it with AI. I understand it takes time. I’m not looking for it to be GTA6 I’m just wanting to build simple games with AI to learn the process

replies.author: Fuzzzy420
replies.body:
Choose a model (local or web).

Install a harness like Claude Code, codex, anti-gravity, Operncode, many more. 

Choose an engine, I would recommend Godot because ai can do everything and read everything. 

Choose a simple idea and discuss it with ai. 
Be aware of affirmation and begin. 

What else you want to know?

comments.author: Brettinabox
comments.body:
I think its a good idea personally. Alot of my recent progress has been not just building a game but also and separately asking questions about professional best practices and how to organize code. There are some crucial extra steps to get the most out of an ai chat so it is definitely not for everyone.

I did a lengthy tutorial in python/pygame a year ago and was proud but very burnt out by the end, took a few weeks. Last couple weeks ive not only built a bigger and more complete game in the first few days, but I understand more about systems and how to break code apart to make it cleaner or less condensed.

replies.author: Aggressive-Fan-4230
replies.body: So what did you do? That was the big part of my question. How did you use AI to do whatever you did

replies.author: Brettinabox
replies.body: Like I said, those extra steps are figuring out the ai part of the situation and knowing how to ask for help in a way thats going to help but also not get you messed up later. Its hard to say, theres no 3 step program or magic solution, asking questions, finding issues with the answers, then asking better questions.

replies.author: Aggressive-Fan-4230
replies.body:
Right, but again I’m asking about how you’re using it and why. I’m looking for resources. You’re giving me “I did it my own way to do something and it gave me what I wanted”.

What I don’t know is what AI did you use, how did it integrate, did you use multiple software for Ai to do characters, sound design, etc or was this all in unity using their AI.

replies.author: Brettinabox
replies.body:
Ive only used google search ai and godot, I think its gemini. I started asking how companies make games, made a game design document, asked questions, reformatted my initial prompt as I went on.

So far all of the assets are code generated and I found some 100% free music or i would probably try to have ai tutor me to make EDM.

Personally its not a deep game though, its got 2D shapes firing and dodging lasers. Lots of procedural generation to keep the fun going hopefully.

replies.author: Brettinabox
replies.body: Learning things like how to make a library, use a decoupled state machine, asking help to make a certain type of trigonometry curve, etc. Is stuff ive asked help with. But things like knowing when the ai doesnt understand the question and give you the wrong implement, being able to underatand what the ai needs to fix the bug, knowing enough about yourself to know how to improve the ai, nobody can teach that.

comments.author: javon27
comments.body: Tell the AI to walk you through it

replies.author: Aggressive-Fan-4230
replies.body: The hard part of this is that AI can rely on limited resources at times for things that are a bit more niche. I was hoping to find a more standard method of doing things

replies.author: javon27
replies.body: Like others have said, I don't think there is one. I'm figuring it out as I go myself. Also, I'm not even bothering to look at the code since that would just slow me down. The key is knowing what to ask for and asking for what you don't know.

replies.author: Aggressive-Fan-4230
replies.body: How are you using AI? Is it integrated in the software you are using to develop the code or is it more like others here saying they google things and google ai gives them recommendations

replies.author: Glorpson
replies.body:
"I was hoping to find a more standard method of doing things" I literally get paid to use AI and try to navigate this question for large organizations. Trust me: there is no standard method of doing things.

If it works, it works (within reasonable safety guardrails). If it works for you, it probably doesn't work for someone else. Sharing AI workflows, tools or processes is incredibly hard... its like looking into the mind of a mad scientist where you back away slowly even if you understand the domain or topic.

Theres shortcuts... overall better ways to get improved results or reduce cost but they're all layerd on scar tissue you just gotta earn mostly. Every time you try a new process you'll question the output and probably spend more time and money on evals trying to figure out if its better until you have a solid gut feeling.

It's getting a lot better with how powerful models are now though.

comments.author: Silly_Suspect_5422
comments.body:
I've had 2 attempts at coding with AI so far. For the first attempt, I wanted to know how to vibecode. I've been writing software for 30 plus years and wanted to see what the new kids were doing. I started out by asking ChatGPT, what vibecoding was, and how I might begin. Just like somebody else already suggested the AI walked me through setting up a development environment on my PC. I then described a super simple game. Actually, it wasn't a game, it was just  a clock face. As the second hand went around, I had flames briefly burst from the tip as it passed 3, 6, 9, and 12. I told the AI what I wanted, it spit out code, and I pasted it in a file and then ran. If there was an eror, I pasted that text into the AI prompt. It gave me more code and I replaced the contents of the file. After a few hours of this, I decided it was for the birds. But at least I knew what I did not want to do.

For my next attempt , I switched to claude. I started out with a lot of long discussions about what I wanted to achieve and how I wanted to get there. In my case, this was a software project that I had started on my own and failed multiple times throughout my life. We decided that baby stepping through the most simple iterations would help me stay on track and produce something before I gave up.

I started out pasting the output from the a I into files just like I had before. But I quickly decided to get Claude to talk me into how to set up Claude code so that it could edit the files directly. ( I also went through a learning curve, trying to understand the difference between what was happening with the context and files between my phone, my PC and the cloud. But eventually I got everything in sync and behaving the way I wanted it to).

We would have long designed discussions where I explained what I wanted , and it explained how it would go about implementing that.  We would also talk about how it would break down the problem into smaller trunks that could be implemented. Each step of the way it would stop and I would look at what changes it had made. A couple of times I caught it doing some silly things and had to straighten him out. I didn't just fix the files myself.I explained what he had done wrong and what I wanted done instead, And then let him fix them. As the code base grew, I created a privare repo on GitHub. There are tools/plugins  which allow claude to interact with github. With a little work , I got him to understand what branching scheme I wanted , and what part he was allowed to play. Nowadays, when I start a new session, it creates a branch off of development, codes and tests there, and then creates a pull request For me to review. At first I was responsible for performing the merge , but i've gotten Comfortable with how it behaves and now let it do the merges.

One of the things I had to do early on was get a handle on what assumptions claude would make. I think we eventually arrived and at an instruction where If it made a reasonable assumption, that was potentially Important , it would tell me about the decision that it had made and the alternatives. For other things, where the right answer was less clear, instead of making a choice, it would stop and ask me for clarification and what I wanted to do.

The other thing which was critical, was getting it to write unit tests. At first , claude would say he had tested things , but when pressed would admit that it had only guessed. I would force him to write controlled unit tests. Today, there are nearly as many lines of code of unit tests as there are real code for the game engine.

Anyway that's what I did. I'm not saying it's the right way.It probably isn't.It was just my way. I hope that it is a closer answer to what you were asking for.

comments.author: EntranceInitial2330
comments.body: This seems like a broad request. Could you please specify what kind of resources you are looking for? Knowing the topic or area of interest would help in providing relevant suggestions.
